summary: Describes the Generic Security Service API, a language-independent interface that lets applications use security services such as authentication without knowing which mechanism does the work. This update refines the earlier version 2 specification. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: GSS-API gives applications one set of calls for checking who a peer is and protecting messages. The application can use different security mechanisms without learning each mechanism's private token format.

subtitle: One interface for applications to establish authenticated peers and protect messages with different security mechanisms.

tldr.problem: Applications need security services without being tied to one cryptographic mechanism or communications protocol.
tldr.mechanism: GSS-API provides common calls for credentials, security contexts, and message protection. Peers exchange opaque tokens that their local GSS-API implementations process.
tldr.outcome: Version 2, update 1 obsoletes RFC 2078 and has been updated by RFC 5554 and RFC 5896. The C language bindings are specified separately in RFC 2744.

today: RFC 2743 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2078. It has been updated by RFC 5554 and RFC 5896; its C language bindings are specified in RFC 2744.

sections.title: The Purpose of GSS-API
sections.content:
The Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) lets a caller request security services through a common interface. A caller can request authentication, message integrity, and optional confidentiality without being written for one underlying security mechanism.

The interface is also independent of the communications protocol and of the relationship between a protocol connection and a security context. Separate specifications define language bindings and the tokens and procedures for particular mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: GSS-API lets an application ask for security without choosing how the security works. Other specifications explain how to connect this interface to a programming language or a particular mechanism.

sections.title: Credentials, Contexts, and Tokens
sections.content:
Credentials give a peer the prerequisites for establishing a security context. Applications refer to credentials through handles, so they do not need direct access to credential contents. A context is established between peers using their local credentials.

Peers exchange tokens to establish and manage a context. After setup, they can exchange per-message tokens that provide integrity and data-origin authentication, with optional confidentiality. Token contents are opaque to the caller, which must transport them and distinguish their purposes.

Several contexts can exist between the same peers, including contexts using different credentials. This can allow a new context to be established while an older credential is nearing expiry. The caller may also provide channel bindings so the mechanism can tie context setup to details of the communications channel.
sections.plainLanguage: Credentials let each side prove an identity. The peers exchange tokens to set up a security context, then use more tokens to protect messages.

sections.title: Names and Mechanisms
sections.content:
GSS-API treats names as opaque because different mechanisms represent and authenticate names in different ways. It provides calls to import, display, compare, release, and duplicate names rather than requiring callers to parse each mechanism's name format.

Callers should use GSS_Compare_name() instead of comparing displayed text, because printable forms can vary. For binary comparisons, GSS_Export_name() produces a flat name with a header identifying the mechanism that authenticated it.

A mechanism is identified by an Object Identifier. The first context-establishment token for Internet standards-track GSS-API mechanisms begins with a mechanism identifier so the receiving implementation can select the right processing mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: A name can have a different form under each security mechanism. GSS-API provides calls to compare names without asking the application to interpret those forms.

sections.title: Establishing a Context and Protecting Messages
sections.content:
A caller starts context setup with GSS_Init_sec_context(); the peer processes its token with GSS_Accept_sec_context(). The peers pass any returned tokens between these calls until the context is complete. A mechanism may need more exchanges, so callers handle GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED by continuing the same call sequence.

Once a context is ready, GSS_GetMIC() creates an integrity token for a message and GSS_VerifyMIC() checks it. Alternatively, GSS_Wrap() protects and encapsulates a message, and GSS_Unwrap() checks and recovers it, including decryption when confidentiality was applied. The caller transports all tokens.

When communication ends, GSS_Delete_sec_context() releases the context. It can optionally return a token asking the peer to release its context too.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers exchange setup tokens until both sides have a context. They then use GSS-API calls to check a message or protect it before sending.

sections.title: Optional Services and Status Results
sections.content:
The initiator can request optional services during context setup, including mutual authentication, delegation, replay detection, out-of-sequence detection, anonymity, integrity, and confidentiality. The mechanism reports which services are available; the caller can stop setup if a requested service is essential but unavailable.

Each call returns a major status for general control flow and a minor status for more detailed, potentially mechanism-specific information. Replay and sequencing results can flag duplicate, old, unsequenced, or missing-predecessor tokens. Detection does not prevent a suspect message from being delivered, so the caller decides what to do with it.

Delegation is allowed only when the application explicitly requests it. Contexts can also be exported and imported between processes on one machine when the mechanism supports that operation.
sections.plainLanguage: An application can ask for extra protections and must check which ones the mechanism provides. Status results report errors or message problems, but the application decides how to respond.

sections.title: Security Depends on the Mechanism and Caller
sections.content:
The interface alone does not provide security or assurance; those properties depend on the underlying mechanism. Callers need to check requested services and returned status values to know what protection is actually available.

Credential access must be restricted by the system below GSS-API, because using a principal's credentials allows a process to assert that principal's identity. Tokens used to transfer a context between processes may contain sensitive data, including cryptographic keys, so applications must protect them while they are transferred.
sections.plainLanguage: GSS-API reports what protection a mechanism provides, but it does not create that protection itself. Systems must restrict access to credentials and protect context-transfer tokens.

messages.label: Context-establishment token
messages.note: GSS_Accept_sec_context returns a token for the initiator.

messages.label: Protected message
messages.note: GSS_Wrap protects the message for transfer.

messages.label: Optional context-deletion token
messages.note: The peer can process it with GSS_Process_context_token.
